course: Pizza Oven Construction - Wood Fired 12 Pizza

lessons.title: Routine Cleaning and Ash Removal
lessons.body:
After every firing, once the oven has cooled completely (at least 12 hours after the last fire), you must remove ash. Ash holds moisture and can corrode the oven floor. Use a metal ash rake and a metal bucket. Never use plastic â it will melt. Scrape the ash from the floor into the bucket. For a 12-pizza oven, you'll typically get 2-3 litres of ash per firing. If you fire daily, remove ash daily. If weekly, remove after each use.

Next, brush the floor with a stiff wire brush. This removes fine ash and carbon deposits. Then wipe with a damp (not wet) cloth. Do not use soap or chemicals â they will soak into the firebrick and taint your pizza. A mixture of 1 part white vinegar to 3 parts water works well for stubborn stains. Rinse with a clean damp cloth and let dry.

Outside the oven, clean the chimney and flue. Remove the chimney cap and use a chimney brush (the same size as your flue, typically 150mm) to scrub the inside. Do this monthly if you use the oven often. Creosote â a black, tar-like substance â builds up and can cause a chimney fire. If you see more than 3mm of creosote, clean immediately.

Check the ash pit or ash drawer if your oven has one. Empty it completely. If ash is left, it can block airflow and make lighting difficult. Also, clean the oven door and its frame. Use a wire brush to remove rust, then wipe with a little cooking oil to protect it.

Finally, inspect the area around the oven. Remove any leaves, wood chips, or flammable materials within 1 metre. Keep the oven area swept. In Africa, where dust and insects are common, cover the oven when not in use with a breathable canvas tarp â not plastic, which traps moisture. A clean oven heats faster, cooks better, and lasts longer.

lessons.title: Inspecting for Cracks and Damage
lessons.body:
Inspect your oven every month, and always after a big firing or a storm. Start with the dome. Look for cracks wider than a matchstick (about 2mm). Hairline cracks (less than 1mm) are normal and not dangerous â they close when the oven heats. But if you can fit a coin into a crack, it needs repair. Use a torch or your phone light to see inside the dome. Pay attention to the top and the joints between bricks.

Check the oven floor (the cooking surface). Cracks here are serious because they let heat escape and can cause uneven baking. Also look for loose bricks or crumbling mortar. Tap the bricks with a screwdriver handle â a hollow sound means the brick has separated from the mortar beneath. Mark any loose areas with chalk.

Examine the chimney and flue. Look for cracks in the mortar joints, rust on metal parts, and any gaps where smoke can escape. A cracked chimney can leak carbon monoxide into your cooking area. Also check the oven door and its hinges. Rust, bent hinges, or a warped door mean heat loss and unsafe operation.

Look at the base and foundation. Cracks in the concrete slab or stand can indicate settling. If the oven is on a trailer, check the welds and tyres. In Africa, termites can damage wooden stands â inspect for mud tubes or soft wood. Also check for water damage: dark stains, moss, or efflorescence (white powder) mean moisture is getting in.

Use a notebook to record what you find and the date. This helps you track changes. If you find a crack wider than 5mm, or if a brick is loose, stop using the oven until repaired. Small cracks can be filled with a fireclay mortar mix (1 part fireclay, 3 parts sand, plus water to a peanut butter consistency). Larger damage needs a professional. Remember: catching a small crack now saves a big rebuild later.

lessons.title: Repairing Mortar Joints and Dome Cracks
lessons.body:
For small cracks (up to 5mm wide) and crumbling mortar joints, you can repair them yourself. You need: fireclay (available at building supply stores), clean sand, a bucket, a trowel, a pointing trowel, a wire brush, and water. Mix 1 part fireclay to 3 parts sand. Add water slowly until the mix is like thick peanut butter â it should hold its shape but be spreadable. Let it sit for 10 minutes, then mix again.

First, clean the crack. Use a wire brush to remove loose mortar, dust, and ash. Then dampen the area with a wet sponge â this helps the new mortar bond. Use a pointing trowel to press the mortar into the crack. Work from the bottom up. Fill the crack completely, then smooth it with the trowel. For deep cracks, fill in layers, letting each layer dry for 30 minutes before adding the next. Do not make the repair thicker than 10mm at a time.

For dome cracks, you may need to remove loose bricks first. Tap them with a hammer â if they move, take them out. Clean the old mortar off the bricks with a chisel and wire brush. Wet the bricks and the socket. Apply mortar to both the brick and the socket, then press the brick back into place. Wiggle it slightly to seat it. Wipe off excess mortar with a damp sponge.

After repair, let the mortar cure slowly. Cover the repaired area with a damp cloth and keep it moist for 24 hours. Then let it air dry for 3 days. Do not fire the oven for at least 7 days. When you first fire it, start with a small fire and increase heat gradually over 2 hours. This prevents steam from cracking the new mortar.

If the crack is larger than 5mm or the dome is sagging, call a professional. In many African cities, you can find masons experienced with wood-fired ovens. Ask for someone who has worked on pizza ovens or kilns. Do not use cement mortar â it cannot handle the heat and will fail quickly.

lessons.title: Replacing Insulation or Chimney Components
lessons.body:
Insulation keeps your oven hot and saves wood. If your oven loses heat quickly (cools below 200Â°C in 2 hours), insulation may be wet or damaged. For a 12-pizza oven, you likely have a layer of ceramic fibre blanket or vermiculite concrete around the dome. To replace, first let the oven cool completely. Remove the outer render or metal cladding. Take out the old insulation â wear gloves and a mask, as ceramic fibres irritate the skin and lungs.

For ceramic fibre blanket, buy 50mm thick, 128kg/mÂ³ density blanket. Wrap the dome in two layers, overlapping the seams. Secure with stainless steel wire or aluminium tape. For vermiculite, mix 1 part Portland cement to 6 parts vermiculite by volume, add water to a thick slurry, and pack it around the dome to a thickness of 100mm. Let it cure for 7 days before firing.

Chimney components: If your chimney is cracked or rusted, replace it. For a 12-pizza oven, a 150mm diameter flue is typical. You can use stainless steel flue pipe (best) or clay flue tiles. If using steel, assemble sections with high-temperature silicone sealant. Secure with self-tapping screws. Install a spark arrestor cap on top. For clay tiles, bed each tile in fireclay mortar, and keep the joints tight.

If your oven has a chimney damper, check that it moves freely. Replace any broken handle or rusted spindle. For the chimney base, repair cracks with fireclay mortar. If the chimney is leaning, brace it with metal straps anchored to the oven stand.

After replacing insulation or chimney parts, do a test fire. Start small, then gradually increase. Check for smoke leaks around joints â if you see smoke, seal with more high-temp silicone. In Africa, source materials from local hardware stores or pottery suppliers. Vermiculite is often sold as horticultural grade â that works. Ceramic fibre blanket may need to be ordered from a kiln supplier. Always wear safety gear.

lessons.title: Winterizing Your Oven
lessons.body:
In many parts of Africa, winter means rain, not snow. But even in dry areas, cold nights and moisture can damage your oven. Winterizing means protecting it from water and freezing temperatures (if you are in highlands like Ethiopia or South Africa). Start by cleaning the oven thoroughly â remove all ash, soot, and food residue. Moisture mixed with ash creates lye, which eats firebrick.

If your oven is outdoors, build a simple roof over it. A sheet of corrugated iron or a canvas tarp on a frame works. Make sure air can circulate â do not wrap in plastic. For the dome, you can apply a waterproof render: mix 1 part cement, 3 parts sand, and a waterproofing additive (available at hardware stores). Apply a 10mm layer over the existing render. This sheds rain.

Check the chimney cap â it should keep rain out but let smoke escape. If your oven has a metal door, oil the hinges and remove any rust with a wire brush, then paint with high-temperature paint. For the floor, place a piece of plywood or a wooden board over the cooking surface to protect it from moisture and pests.

If freezing temperatures are possible, drain any water lines (if you have a water jacket). For the oven itself, no water should be inside. If the oven is not used for weeks, place a small container of charcoal or silica gel inside to absorb moisture. Change it monthly.

Before winter, do a full inspection as in Lesson 2. Repair any cracks now. After winter, remove the cover, clean again, and do a small test fire to drive out moisture. Start with a very small fire (just paper and kindling) for 1 hour, then increase. Sudden high heat can crack a damp oven. In Africa, the rainy season is your 'winter' â prepare before the first rains.

lessons.title: Annual Safety Checks
lessons.body:
Once a year, do a thorough safety check. This prevents fires, carbon monoxide poisoning, and structural failure. Start with the chimney and flue. Use a mirror and torch to inspect the inside. Creosote should be less than 3mm thick. If more, clean with a chimney brush. Check for cracks, loose joints, and rust. Replace any damaged sections. Ensure the chimney extends at least 600mm above the roof and has a spark arrestor.

Check the oven door and its seal. A poor seal lets heat escape and smoke into your cooking area. Replace the door gasket if it is frayed or hardened. For metal doors, check hinges and latches â tighten screws and oil moving parts. If the door is warped, replace it.

Inspect the oven structure. Look for cracks in the dome, floor, and stand. Tap bricks with a screwdriver â hollow sounds mean loose bricks. Check the foundation for settling or cracks. If the oven is on a trailer, check wheel bearings, tyres, and lights. For a fixed oven, ensure it is anchored to the ground.

Check for fire safety. Keep a fire extinguisher (dry powder, 2kg minimum) within 3 metres of the oven. Test it annually. Clear any dry grass, wood, or rubbish within 2 metres. Ensure the oven is not under a tree or near a thatched roof. Have a bucket of sand or water nearby for emergencies.

Finally, check carbon monoxide risks. Never use the oven in an enclosed space without ventilation. If you have a covered outdoor kitchen, install a CO detector. Test it monthly. Also, check gas lines if you have a gas-assisted oven â look for leaks with soapy water. Record all checks in a logbook. Date, what you checked, what you fixed. This proves you maintain your oven and helps spot trends. Do this every year, and your oven will last 20+ years.

quiz.q: How soon after the last fire should you remove ash from the oven?
quiz.explanation: Ash should be removed only after the oven has cooled completely, at least 12 hours after the last fire, to avoid burns and damage.

quiz.q: What tool is best for removing ash from a pizza oven?
quiz.explanation: A metal ash rake is durable and heat-resistant, while plastic can melt and vacuums can spread ash.

quiz.q: How much ash does a 12-pizza oven typically produce per firing?
quiz.explanation: A typical 12-pizza oven produces 2-3 litres of ash per firing, which should be removed regularly.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean stubborn stains on the oven floor?
quiz.explanation: A mixture of 1 part white vinegar to 3 parts water is safe and effective for cleaning the firebrick without chemicals that taint food.

quiz.q: How often should you clean the chimney if you use the oven often?
quiz.explanation: Monthly cleaning of the chimney prevents creosote buildup, which can cause chimney fires.

quiz.q: What is creosote?
quiz.explanation: Creosote is a black, tar-like substance that builds up in chimneys and is highly flammable.

quiz.q: What size crack in the dome is considered normal and not dangerous?
quiz.explanation: Hairline cracks less than 1mm are normal and close when the oven heats; wider cracks need repair.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a brick has separated from the mortar?
options: B) It sounds hollow when tapped
D) It is loose to touch
quiz.explanation: A hollow sound when tapping with a screwdriver handle indicates the brick has separated from the mortar.

quiz.q: What is a sign of water damage in the oven?
quiz.explanation: Efflorescence, a white powder, indicates moisture is getting into the masonry.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a crack wider than 5mm?
options: C) Stop using the oven until repaired
quiz.explanation: Cracks wider than 5mm are structural and require professional repair; continuing to use the oven can worsen damage.

quiz.q: What is the correct mix for fireclay mortar?
options: A) 1 part fireclay to 3 parts sand
B) 1 part cement to 3 parts sand
C) 1 part fireclay to 1 part sand
D) 3 parts fireclay to 1 part sand
quiz.explanation: The standard mix is 1 part fireclay to 3 parts sand, mixed with water to a peanut butter consistency.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before firing the oven after repairing mortar?
quiz.explanation: After repairing mortar, wait at least 7 days before firing to allow proper curing and prevent steam cracks.

quiz.q: What should you do before applying new mortar to a crack?
quiz.explanation: Dampening the area with a wet sponge helps the new mortar bond better.

quiz.q: What type of mortar should never be used for oven repairs?
quiz.explanation: Cement mortar cannot withstand high heat and will fail quickly; always use fireclay mortar.

quiz.q: What is a sign that insulation needs replacing?
options: B) Oven cools below 200Â°C in 2 hours
quiz.explanation: If the oven loses heat quickly, insulation may be wet or damaged and needs replacement.

quiz.q: What is the recommended density for ceramic fibre blanket insulation?
quiz.explanation: 128kg/mÂ³ density ceramic fibre blanket is suitable for wood-fired ovens.

quiz.q: What is the typical diameter of a flue for a 12-pizza oven?
quiz.explanation: A 150mm diameter flue is standard for a 12-pizza oven.

quiz.q: What should you use to seal joints in a stainless steel chimney?
quiz.explanation: High-temperature silicone sealant is designed to withstand the heat of a chimney.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio for vermiculite insulation mix?
options: A) 1 part cement to 6 parts vermiculite
B) 1 part cement to 3 parts vermiculite
C) 1 part vermiculite to 6 parts cement
D) 1 part sand to 6 parts vermiculite
quiz.explanation: The standard mix is 1 part Portland cement to 6 parts vermiculite by volume.

quiz.q: Why should you not wrap the oven in plastic for winter?
quiz.explanation: Plastic traps moisture, which can damage the oven; use a breathable canvas tarp instead.

quiz.q: What should you place inside the oven to absorb moisture during long storage?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal or silica gel absorbs moisture and prevents dampness inside the oven.

quiz.q: What is the first step in winterizing your oven?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes ash and soot, preventing lye formation and moisture damage.

quiz.q: How thick should a waterproof render be applied?
quiz.explanation: A 10mm layer of waterproof render effectively sheds rain.

quiz.q: What should you do before the first fire after winter?
options: B) Start a small fire and increase gradually
quiz.explanation: Starting with a small fire and increasing gradually drives out moisture without cracking the oven.

quiz.q: How often should you do a full safety check on your oven?
quiz.explanation: An annual safety check ensures all components are in good condition and prevents accidents.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended creosote thickness in a chimney?
quiz.explanation: Creosote should be less than 3mm thick; more than that increases chimney fire risk.

quiz.q: What type of fire extinguisher is recommended for a pizza oven?
quiz.explanation: A dry powder extinguisher (2kg minimum) is effective for wood fires and safe near ovens.

quiz.q: How far should flammable materials be kept from the oven?
quiz.explanation: Keep at least 2 metres clearance to prevent accidental fires.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a poor oven door seal?
options: B) Smoke escapes into cooking area
quiz.explanation: Smoke escaping indicates a poor seal, which wastes heat and can be a health hazard.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a logbook of maintenance?
options: B) To track changes and prove maintenance
quiz.explanation: A logbook helps spot trends and provides a record of proper maintenance.
